title: How to Stay Composed at Work
tagline: Notice your triggers, calm yourself in the moment and stay steady with difficult people, heavy workloads, criticism and crises.
description:
Everyone loses their calm sometimes: an angry customer, a sharp email from the boss, a blame message on the office WhatsApp group or a pile of deadlines. Composure is not about having no feelings. It is the skill of noticing what is happening inside you and choosing your response on purpose. This quest teaches that skill in small, practical steps.

**Basic stages (free):**

- **What composure is:** the stress loop, your personal triggers and the early signals in your body.
- **Calm tools for the moment:** slow breathing, the STOP pause, holding phrases and reframing hot thoughts.
- **Difficult people:** angry customers, harsh managers, rude emails and heated group chats.

**Advanced stages (Premium):**

- **Pressure:** turning workload into a plan, agreeing priorities and saying no politely.
- **Criticism and mistakes:** hearing feedback without taking it personally, owning errors and bouncing back.
- **Lasting resilience and calm leadership:** rest, routine, boundaries, support networks and keeping a team steady in a crisis.

This is a workplace skills course, not therapy. If stress, anxiety or low mood stays with you for weeks, please speak to a doctor or a qualified professional. Follow Maham, a customer care officer in Lahore, from her worst call to leading her team through a crisis.
audience: Students and fresh graduates starting their first jobs or internships
Customer service, call centre and front-desk staff who deal with upset people every day
Office staff who juggle deadlines, demanding managers and busy group chats
Small-business owners who face difficult customers and long days alone
New team leads and supervisors who want to stay steady and keep their team calm
outcomes: Explain composure and the stress loop, and name your own triggers and early body signals
Use quick calm tools in the moment: slow breathing, the STOP pause, holding phrases and reframing
Stay calm with angry customers, harsh managers, rude messages and heated group chats
Turn heavy workloads into a sorted plan, agree priorities and say no politely
Hear criticism without taking it personally, own mistakes professionally and bounce back from setbacks
Build lasting resilience through rest, routine, boundaries and support, and lead a team calmly in a crisis

quest.name: Operation Steady Hands
quest.premise: Maham Siddiqui is a bright customer care officer at Zaitoon Electronics in Lahore, but one bad call ends with her shouting at a customer in front of the whole floor. With her mentor Nadia, an HR coach in Islamabad, her sometimes sharp supervisor Kamran, the nervous intern Ali and her friend Usman, who runs a print shop in Faisalabad, she learns to keep her calm from the first trigger to her first crisis as team lead. Clear each stage and earn steady hands.

sessions.title: What Composure Is: Noticing Your Triggers and Early Body Signals
sessions.summary: Learn what composure really means at work and why it matters for trust, decisions and your own peace of mind. You will spot the situations that set you off and the early signals in your body, so you can catch a reaction before it catches you.
objectives: Explain composure in plain words and how it differs from hiding your feelings
Describe the stress loop from trigger to body signal, thought, reaction and result
Name your own common triggers at work
Notice early body signals such as a tight jaw, hot face or fast typing
Keep a simple trigger log to learn your own patterns

cards.title: The call that went wrong
cards.setting: Zaitoon Electronics customer care centre, Lahore. A Monday afternoon after a long queue of calls.

lines.text: Welcome to the Steady Hands quest. Your first stop is a busy customer care desk in Lahore, where a calm young officer has just lost her temper.
Sir, I have told you three times, the technician will come tomorrow! Please stop shouting at me!
The customer hangs up. Maham's hands are shaking. Her supervisor, Kamran, looks over from his desk.
Maham, the whole floor heard that. We cannot speak to customers like this.
I know. I did not even feel it coming. One second I was fine, the next second I was shouting.
It almost always feels like that, Maham. But your body was sending signals long before you shouted. Let us learn to read them.
Signals? Like what?
A tight jaw, a hot face, typing harder on the keyboard. Notice those early, and you get a choice. That choice is what we call composure.

scenes.heading: It is not having no feelings
scenes.narration: Composure does not mean you never feel angry, worried or hurt. Everyone does. It means your feelings do not take the steering wheel at work.

scenes.heading: Notice
scenes.narration: The first step is simply noticing. 'My face is getting hot. I am getting irritated.' Naming it quietly in your head already slows things down.

scenes.heading: Pause
scenes.narration: Next comes a short pause, even a few seconds. A slow breath out, a sip of water or a quiet 'let me check' gives you room to think.

scenes.heading: Choose
scenes.narration: Then you choose your response on purpose: what to say, how to say it and when. You act from your values, not from the heat of the moment.

scenes.heading: Recover
scenes.narration: Finally, you recover. Even calm people slip sometimes. Composure includes cooling down, repairing if needed and getting back to steady work.

cards.title: The stress loop
cards.caption: A trigger sets off signals in the body, then thoughts, then a reaction. The result often becomes the next trigger. You can break the loop at any point.

items.label: Trigger
items.detail: Something happens: a shouting customer, a sharp email, a missed deadline.

items.label: Body signal
items.detail: Your body reacts first: tight jaw, hot face, fast heartbeat, clenched hands.

items.label: Thought
items.detail: Your mind tells a quick story: 'He thinks I am useless' or 'This is not fair.'

items.label: Reaction
items.detail: You act on the story: snap back, go silent, type an angry reply.

items.label: Result
items.detail: The situation gets better or worse, and the result often sets off the next trigger.

cards.question: Which description best matches composure at work?
options: Never showing any feeling, whatever happens around you
Feeling what you feel, but choosing how you respond
Agreeing with everyone so that nobody gets upset
Staying quiet in every difficult conversation at work
cards.explanation: Composure is not hiding or switching off your feelings. It means you notice them and still choose your words and actions on purpose. Staying quiet or agreeing with everyone can be just as unhelpful as shouting.

cards.title: Why composure matters at work
cards.body:
Composure is a work skill, just like writing a clear email or using a spreadsheet. It helps in many ways:

- **Trust:** customers, managers and colleagues trust people who stay steady when things go wrong.
- **Better decisions:** when you are calmer, you can think more clearly about what to do next.
- **Fewer regrets:** a calm reply rarely needs an apology later. An angry one often does.
- **Your reputation:** people remember how you behaved on the hard day, not only the easy days.
- **Your own peace:** going home without replaying an argument all evening is worth a lot.

The good news is that composure can be practised. Nobody is born with it fully formed.

cards.back: An angry customer or colleague raises their voice, and your body reacts as if you are under attack.
A task you finished is suddenly changed, or a new deadline appears at 5 pm.
Someone points out your mistake in front of the team or on a group chat.
Your idea is skipped in a meeting, or your messages get no reply for days.
The system freezes, the printer jams or the internet drops just before a deadline.
You are held responsible for something that was not your fault.

cards.title: How a reaction builds
cards.caption: Most reactions climb in steps. The earlier you notice, the easier it is to stop.

items.label: A small sign
items.detail: Jaw tightens, shoulders lift, breath gets short.

items.label: Heat rises
items.detail: Face feels hot, heartbeat speeds up, hands get restless.

items.label: Thoughts race
items.detail: You start building an argument in your head while the other person is still talking.

items.label: Behaviour changes
items.detail: Voice gets louder or sharper, typing gets faster, you interrupt.

items.label: The snap
items.detail: You say or send something you would not say on a calm day.

cards.title: Hot face in the team meeting
cards.situation: In the Monday team meeting, Kamran puts a complaint report on the screen and asks, 'Who handled this customer?' It was Maham. She feels her face go hot and her heart start to pound. Everyone turns to look at her.

choices.text: Notice the heat, take one slow breath out, and say: 'That was my call. Can I explain what happened and what I would do differently?'
choices.outcome: Maham stays steady and owns it. Kamran relaxes, and the meeting becomes about fixing the problem, not about blame. Her colleagues see someone who can handle pressure.

choices.text: Stay silent and hope Kamran moves on, then complain about him to a colleague afterwards.
choices.outcome: Avoiding the moment keeps things quiet for now, but the complaint is not resolved and Maham replays it all evening. Talking behind Kamran's back may also come back to her.

choices.text: Say quickly, 'It was not my fault, the customer was impossible and the system was down.'
choices.outcome: Maham speaks from the heat of the moment. It sounds like an excuse, Kamran pushes harder, and the meeting turns tense.

cards.title: Trigger, body signal or reaction?
cards.prompt: Sort each item into the part of the stress loop it belongs to.

items.text: A customer starts shouting on the phone
Your jaw tightens and shoulders rise
You type a reply in capital letters
Your manager changes the deadline to today
Your face feels hot and your heart races
You interrupt and raise your voice
A colleague takes credit for your work
Your breathing gets short and fast

cards.title: Composed or just bottling it up?
cards.caption: Hiding feelings is not the same as handling them. Composure is honest and calm; bottling up is silent and tense.

items.label: Inside
items.left: You notice the feeling and name it
items.right: You push the feeling down and pretend it is not there

items.label: Outside
items.left: Calm voice, clear words, steady pace
items.right: Tight smile, short answers, or sudden silence

items.label: Later
items.left: You may talk it through or let it go
items.right: It leaks out later as a snap at someone else

items.label: Over time
items.left: You learn your patterns and get steadier
items.right: Pressure builds and small things feel huge

cards.question: Maham notices she has started typing very hard on her keyboard while reading a customer complaint. What is this most likely to be?
options: A sign that her keyboard needs replacing soon
Proof that the customer is being unreasonable
A reason to send her reply as fast as she can
An early body signal that irritation is building
cards.explanation: Changes in behaviour such as typing harder, tapping a foot or clenching a pen are often early signals of stress or irritation. Spotting them is a chance to pause before replying.

cards.title: Maham's trigger log
cards.body:
Nadia asks Maham to keep a small log for one week. She writes a line in a notebook whenever she feels her calm slipping:

| Day | Trigger | Body signal | What I did |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mon | Customer shouted | Hot face | Shouted back |
| Tue | Kamran changed a task at 5 pm | Tight jaw | Sighed loudly |
| Wed | System froze mid-call | Fast breathing | Apologised to customer, stayed calm |
| Thu | Team chat blamed our desk | Shaking hands | Did not reply for an hour, then replied politely |

By Friday she sees a pattern: shouting and last-minute changes are her biggest triggers, and her face gets hot first. Now she knows what to watch for.

cards.title: Go gently, and know when to ask for help
cards.body: Noticing your triggers can bring up uncomfortable feelings. Be patient with yourself: this course teaches workplace skills, not therapy. If stress, worry or low mood stays with you for weeks, affects your sleep or your daily life, or feels too heavy to carry, please speak to a doctor or a qualified mental health professional. Asking for help is a sensible, strong step.

cards.title: What is your body telling you?
cards.prompt: Match each early signal with a calm first move.

pairs.right: Let your teeth part and relax your face for a moment
Take one slow breath and let the out-breath be longer
Pause before speaking and lower your voice a little
Stop typing, save it as a draft and reread it later
Drop your shoulders and put both feet on the floor

cards.title: Remember from The Signal Room
items: Composure means feeling your feelings but choosing your response.
Reactions follow a loop: trigger, body signal, thought, reaction, result.
Your body usually warns you before you snap: tight jaw, hot face, fast breath.
Hiding feelings is not composure; it often leaks out later.
A simple trigger log shows your personal patterns in about a week.
If stress or low mood stays for weeks, speak to a doctor or qualified professional.

cards.prompt: Think about the last time you lost your calm at work, college or home. What was the trigger, and what did your body feel first? Write down one signal you will watch for this week.

quiz.question: What does composure at work mean?
options: Never feeling angry or upset at work
Choosing your response even when feelings are strong
Always agreeing to avoid an argument
Keeping a fixed smile on your face whatever happens to you
quiz.explanation: Composure means you still feel things but you choose how to respond. It is not the absence of feelings or the habit of agreeing with everyone.

quiz.question: In the stress loop, what usually comes straight after a trigger?
options: The final result of the situation
A carefully planned, polite and well-thought-out reply
A body signal such as a hot face or tight jaw
An apology to the other person
quiz.explanation: After a trigger, the body often reacts first, before we have had time to think. Noticing these signals gives us a chance to pause.

quiz.question: Which of these is an example of a workplace trigger?
options: Your shoulders rising slowly up towards your ears
Taking a slow breath before you speak
Writing a line in your trigger log
Your manager moving a deadline to today
quiz.explanation: A trigger is the event that sets off the reaction. A deadline suddenly moved to today is an event; rising shoulders are a body signal; slow breathing and logging are calm tools.

quiz.question: Why is it useful to notice early body signals?
options: They give you a chance to pause before you react
They prove that the other person is wrong
They mean you should leave the job
They show that you should reply as fast as you possibly can
quiz.explanation: Early signals are a warning light. When you notice them, you can slow down and choose a calm response instead of reacting on autopilot.

quiz.question: Ahmed smiles tightly, says 'fine' to everything and then snaps at his younger brother at home. What is he most likely doing at work?
options: Showing excellent composure
Practising the pause technique
Bottling up his feelings
Using his trigger log well
quiz.explanation: A tight smile and short answers followed by a snap later usually mean feelings are being pushed down, not handled. Composure is calmer and more honest.

quiz.question: Which body signal is a common early sign of irritation?
options: Feeling sleepy after lunch
A jaw that feels tight
Feeling hungry before dinner
Cold hands on a winter morning
quiz.explanation: A tight jaw is a common early sign that tension is building. The others usually have everyday causes unrelated to stress at work.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a trigger log?
options: To collect evidence against difficult colleagues and customers
To show your manager how hard your job is
To prove that customers are rude
To spot your own patterns of triggers and signals
quiz.explanation: A trigger log is a private learning tool. Over a week or two it shows which situations set you off and which signals come first.

quiz.question: Which statement about composure is true?
options: It is a skill that improves with practice
You are either born with it or you are not
Only managers need it
It means never making a mistake
quiz.explanation: Composure is a learnable skill. Like any skill, it gets stronger the more you practise noticing, pausing and choosing.

quiz.question: Saima has felt anxious and low most days for over a month, and she is sleeping badly. What is the most sensible next step?
options: Keep it to herself until it passes
Practise breathing harder and ignore the rest
Speak to a doctor or qualified professional
Take on extra work to stay distracted
quiz.explanation: Workplace calm tools help with everyday stress, but persistent anxiety, low mood or poor sleep deserves proper support from a doctor or qualified professional.

quiz.question: Maham notices her face getting hot while a customer complains. Which response shows composure?
options: Interrupt to explain the rules before the customer finishes
Hang up and call back when she feels calmer
Tell the customer that shouting is not allowed
Breathe out, let the customer finish, then answer calmly
quiz.explanation: Noticing the signal and pausing lets her listen fully and reply calmly. Interrupting or hanging up usually makes the customer angrier.

sessions.title: In-the-Moment Calm Tools: Breathing, Pausing and Reframing
sessions.summary: Build a small toolkit you can use in seconds, at your desk or on a call: a slow out-breath, a short pause before you reply, holding phrases that buy you time and a simple way to reframe unhelpful thoughts. Your win: replying to a sharp message without regret.
objectives: Use a slow breathing pattern quietly at your desk or during a call
Apply the STOP pause before replying to a tense message or comment
Use short holding phrases to buy time politely
Reframe a hot thought into a fairer, calmer one
Choose the right calm tool for the time and intensity of the moment

cards.title: The email in capital letters
cards.setting: Zaitoon Electronics, Lahore. 6:40 pm, as Maham is packing up to leave.

lines.text: Maham's phone buzzes. It is an email from Kamran with the subject line: WHY IS THE COMPLAINT SHEET STILL NOT UPDATED?
I updated it at four o'clock! He did not even check. I am writing back right now.
Baji, maybe wait? Last time someone replied to him angrily, it became a big drama.
But if I do not reply, he will think I am lazy.
You can reply, Maham. The question is when and how. Can you give it two minutes and one slow breath first?
Two minutes. Fine. I will breathe and then read it again.
Good. Now ask yourself: is there another way to read his email? Maybe he opened an old file. Maybe he is under pressure from his own boss.
Okay. I will write: 'Sir, I updated it at 4 pm. Here is the link to the latest version.' Short and calm.

scenes.heading: Stop
scenes.narration: When you feel the heat rise, stop what you are doing for a moment. Take your hands off the keyboard or let the other person finish speaking.

scenes.heading: Breathe out slowly
scenes.narration: Take a normal breath in, then breathe out a little more slowly than usual. Many people find a long, gentle out-breath helps them feel steadier.

scenes.heading: Name it
scenes.narration: Say to yourself, 'I am feeling angry' or 'I am feeling embarrassed.' Putting a simple name on the feeling often makes it feel more manageable.

scenes.heading: Reframe
scenes.narration: Ask, 'Is there another way to see this?' A sharp email may come from someone rushed, not someone who dislikes you.

scenes.heading: Choose the next step
scenes.narration: Decide one small, calm action: reply later, ask a question, or say 'Let me check and come back to you.'

cards.title: STOP: a pause you can use anywhere
cards.caption: Four quick steps you can do in under a minute, without anyone noticing.

items.label: S: Stop
items.detail: Freeze for a moment. Do not type, send or speak yet.

items.label: T: Take a breath
items.detail: One or two slow breaths, with the out-breath a little longer.

items.label: O: Observe
items.detail: What am I feeling? What is actually happening? What do I want to happen next?

items.label: P: Proceed
items.detail: Act on purpose: a calm reply, a question or a short delay.

cards.question: Maham reads a sharp email and feels like replying straight away in capital letters. What is the best first step?
options: Reply immediately so Kamran knows she is right
Forward the email to her colleagues to get their support
Pause, take a slow breath and reread the email before replying
Ignore the email completely and never mention it
cards.explanation: A short pause and a slow breath give Maham time to read the email again and reply calmly with facts. Replying in anger or forwarding it to others often makes the problem bigger.

cards.title: Breathing you can do at your desk
cards.body:
You do not need a quiet room or special training. Try this:

1. Sit or stand normally, with both feet on the floor.
2. Breathe in gently through your nose for a slow count of about four.
3. Breathe out gently for a slow count of about six, as if cooling a cup of chai.
4. Repeat two or three times.

The exact numbers do not matter. What matters is a slow, comfortable rhythm with a slightly longer out-breath. Nobody on a call can tell you are doing it.

Keep it gentle. If you ever feel dizzy or uncomfortable, stop and breathe normally. If you have a breathing or heart condition, follow your doctor's advice.

cards.title: Pause before you reply
cards.prompt: Put these steps for answering a heated message in a sensible order.
steps: Notice the heat: 'I am annoyed by this message'
Take your hands off the keyboard and breathe out slowly
Reread the message and look only for the facts
Write a short draft that answers the facts
Wait a few minutes, reread the draft and soften any sharp words
Send the reply, or call the person if it is complicated

cards.title: Hot thought or fairer thought?
cards.caption: Reframing does not mean pretending all is fine. It means finding a fairer, more useful way to see the same facts.

items.label: A sharp email
items.right: 'He may be rushed. I will reply with the facts.'

items.label: A customer shouts
items.right: 'She is upset about her fridge, not about me.'

items.label: A plan changes
items.right: 'Some parts can still be used. What is the new priority?'

items.label: You made a mistake
items.right: 'I made one mistake. What is the fix?'

cards.title: The misprinted wedding cards
cards.situation: At Tariq Printers in Faisalabad, a customer storms in with a box of wedding cards. The groom's name is spelt wrong. He says loudly, 'You people are careless! The wedding is in five days!' Usman, the owner, feels his heart racing. He checked the proof himself and the customer had approved that spelling in writing.

choices.text: Take a slow breath, say 'I can see this is really stressful with the wedding so close,' then calmly check the signed proof together and talk about a fast reprint.
choices.outcome: The customer calms down when he feels heard. Together they see the spelling came from the approved proof. Usman offers a fast reprint at a fair price, and the customer leaves relieved.

choices.text: Stay quiet, let him finish, then say 'Please show me the proof,' without much warmth.
choices.outcome: Things do not get worse, but the customer still feels he is not being heard. It takes longer to reach a solution.

choices.text: Wave the signed proof in his face and say, 'This is your mistake, not mine!'
choices.outcome: Usman is right about the facts, but the customer feels humiliated. He leaves angry and tells his family to use another printer.

cards.back: Breathe out a little more slowly than you breathe in, two or three times.
Press both feet into the floor and notice the feeling. It brings your attention back to the present.
Silently name five things you can see around you. It slows racing thoughts.
Lift them slightly, then let them drop. Unclench your jaw at the same time.
A slow sip of water is a natural, polite way to take a short pause.
Say 'Give me two minutes' and take a short walk or wash your face before you return.

cards.title: Which calm tool, when?
cards.caption: Pick a tool to fit the moment: how strong the feeling is and how much time you have.

items.label: Strong feeling, no time
items.detail: Long out-breath and a holding phrase: 'Let me check that for you.'

items.label: Strong feeling, some time
items.detail: Step away for a few minutes, then reframe before you reply.

items.label: Mild feeling, no time
items.detail: Relax your shoulders, unclench your jaw and keep going.

items.label: Mild feeling, some time
items.detail: Write the hot thought down and find a fairer version.

cards.question: Which of these is a good holding phrase to buy time politely?
options: 'Why are you always asking me this?'
'Let me check that and come back to you by 3 pm.'
'Fine. Whatever you want.'
'I am too busy to deal with this now.'
cards.explanation: A holding phrase gives you time to think while still sounding helpful. Giving a clear time ('by 3 pm') shows the person you will follow through.

cards.title: Reframing in action: Maham's three thoughts
cards.body:
Nadia asks Maham to write down her hot thoughts from one day, then find a fairer version of each:

- **Hot:** 'Kamran never trusts my work.' **Fairer:** 'He checked an old file once. Most weeks he accepts my reports without changes.'
- **Hot:** 'This customer hates me.' **Fairer:** 'He is angry about a late repair. I can help with that.'
- **Hot:** 'I will never get through this queue.' **Fairer:** 'The queue is long, but I can take one call at a time and ask for help at 5 pm if needed.'

The facts did not change. But the fairer thoughts made it easier for Maham to stay calm and act.

cards.title: Holding phrases that buy you time
cards.body:
Keep a few calm phrases ready, so you do not have to think of them under pressure:

- 'Let me check that and come back to you.'
- 'I want to get this right. Can I have ten minutes?'
- 'Can you tell me a bit more about what happened?'
- 'I hear you. Let us see what we can do.'

Then make sure you really do come back. A holding phrase builds trust only if you follow through.

cards.title: Hot thought to fairer thought
cards.prompt: Match each hot thought with a fairer, calmer way of seeing it.

pairs.right: 'One person was rude today. Others thanked me this week.'
'This is a problem. Problems have next steps.'
'I do not know why she did it yet. I can ask.'
'Everyone makes mistakes. What matters is how I fix them.'
'A calm reply in ten minutes is better than a sharp one now.'

cards.title: Remember from The Pause Bridge
items: A short pause between the trigger and your reply is your most useful tool.
A slow, gentle out-breath can help you feel steadier; keep it comfortable.
Use STOP: Stop, Take a breath, Observe, Proceed.
Holding phrases buy time politely; always follow through.
Reframing finds a fairer view of the same facts; it is not pretending.
Match the tool to the moment: how strong the feeling is and how much time you have.

cards.prompt: Write down one holding phrase you will use this week and one hot thought you often have at work or college. What is a fairer version of that thought?

quiz.question: What does the 'T' in the STOP pause stand for?
options: Talk it through
Type your reply
Tell your manager
Take a breath
quiz.explanation: STOP stands for Stop, Take a breath, Observe and Proceed. The breath gives you a moment to think before you act.

quiz.question: Which breathing pattern does this course suggest for staying steady at your desk?
options: A slow, gentle rhythm with a slightly longer out-breath
Holding your breath for as long as you can
Breathing very fast for one minute
Breathing only through your mouth in big, quick gulps of air
quiz.explanation: A slow, comfortable rhythm with a slightly longer out-breath is simple and quiet. Keep it gentle and stop if you feel uncomfortable.

quiz.question: What is reframing?
options: Pretending a problem does not exist
Finding a fairer, more useful way to see the same facts
Blaming someone else for the problem so you feel less guilty
Changing the facts so you look better
quiz.explanation: Reframing keeps the facts but changes the story we tell about them, so we can respond more calmly and usefully.

quiz.question: A customer says, 'Your company is useless!' Which reframe is the most helpful for the officer on the call?
options: 'He is right, I am useless at this job.'
'He is just a rude person, so I can ignore what he says to me.'
'He is upset about his problem. I can help with that.'
'I should tell him how rude he is being.'
quiz.explanation: Seeing the anger as being about the problem, not about you personally, makes it easier to stay calm and focus on helping.

quiz.question: Why should you follow through after using a holding phrase such as 'Let me check and come back to you'?
options: Because the phrase only builds trust if you do come back
Because it is a legal requirement in every company
Because it lets you put off dealing with the problem for longer
Because the other person will forget anyway
quiz.explanation: A holding phrase is a promise. Keeping it builds trust; breaking it makes the next conversation harder.

quiz.question: You feel a strong flash of anger but have no time, because a customer is waiting on the line. Which tool fits best?
options: Write a full page about your feelings
A slow out-breath and a short holding phrase
Leave your desk for twenty minutes
Put the customer on hold without saying anything
quiz.explanation: When the feeling is strong and time is short, a quick breath and a holding phrase help you stay steady without leaving the customer waiting.

quiz.question: Ali wants to send an angry reply on the office chat. Which order of steps is best?
options: Send, then breathe, then apologise
Write a long reply, send it, then reread it
Breathe, reread the message, draft a short reply, wait, then send
Forward the message to a few friends first and ask them what to say back
quiz.explanation: Pausing, rereading for facts and waiting before sending helps you reply with a clear head. Sending first and thinking later often leads to regret.

quiz.question: Which of these is a quick, quiet calm tool you can use during a meeting?
options: Leaving the meeting without a word
Telling the speaker to calm down
Checking social media on your phone under the table for a while
Relaxing your shoulders and unclenching your jaw
quiz.explanation: Small physical resets like relaxing your shoulders and jaw are quiet and can be done without anyone noticing.

quiz.question: Which statement about naming your feelings is most accurate?
options: Naming a feeling makes it grow stronger
Naming a feeling quietly can make it feel more manageable
You should always announce your feelings to the whole team
Only weak people need to name their feelings
quiz.explanation: Quietly saying 'I am feeling angry' helps you step back from the feeling a little, which makes it easier to choose your response.

quiz.question: Usman knows the customer approved the wrong spelling in writing. What is the calmest helpful approach?
options: Prove the customer wrong loudly so everyone in the shop hears
Refuse to discuss anything at all until the customer apologises to him
Acknowledge the stress, check the proof together and offer options
Reprint everything for free without checking anything
quiz.explanation: Acknowledging feelings first lowers the heat. Checking the facts together keeps it fair, and offering options moves things forward.

sessions.title: Staying Calm with Difficult People: Angry Customers, Harsh Bosses and Rude Messages
sessions.summary: Use your calm tools with real people: an angry customer at the counter, a manager who speaks harshly and rude messages on email or WhatsApp groups. You will learn to listen first, separate tone from content and move heated chats to the right place. Your win: one difficult conversation handled with dignity.
objectives: Calm an angry customer by listening, acknowledging and offering a next step
Separate a harsh tone from the useful content of a manager's feedback
Reply to rude emails and group messages without adding fuel
Move a heated group chat to a private message or call
Recognise when behaviour crosses a line and needs reporting, not just calm

cards.title: The broken washing machine
cards.setting: Zaitoon Electronics service counter, Lahore. A hot Saturday morning with a long queue.

lines.text: A man pushes to the front of the queue holding a repair slip. His washing machine has broken down again, two weeks after the last repair.
Assalam o alaikum, sir. How can I help?
He slaps the slip on the counter. 'This is the third time! My wife is washing clothes by hand. Your people are cheats!'
My face is getting hot. Long breath out. He is angry about the machine, not about me.
Sir, I am sorry. Two weeks after a repair, and broken again. That is really frustrating, especially with a family at home.
The man's voice drops a little. 'Yes. It is very frustrating.'
Let me check your file now. I can see the earliest technician slot and tell you exactly when it is.
Did you see that? You did not argue and you did not give in. You listened, you named his feeling and you moved to a next step.

scenes.heading: It is usually not about you
scenes.narration: Most anger at work is about a problem: a late delivery, a broken product, pressure from above. Remembering this helps you not take it personally.

scenes.heading: Listen first
scenes.narration: Let the person finish. Interrupting to explain or defend usually raises the temperature. Listening fully often lowers it.

scenes.heading: Lower your voice
scenes.narration: When someone gets louder, try speaking a little slower and softer. People often match the tone you set, without realising it.

scenes.heading: Acknowledge
scenes.narration: Name what they feel and why: 'I can see this has been frustrating.' Acknowledging is not the same as agreeing that you are at fault.

scenes.heading: Move to a next step
scenes.narration: Offer something concrete: a time, an action, a person who can help. A clear next step gives the anger somewhere to go.

cards.title: Calming an angry customer
cards.caption: Five steps you can follow at a counter, on the phone or in a chat.

items.label: Listen
items.detail: Let them finish without interrupting. Take notes if it helps.

items.label: Acknowledge
items.detail: Name the feeling: 'I understand why you are upset.'

items.label: Clarify
items.detail: Ask one or two questions to get the facts right.

items.label: Offer a next step
items.detail: Say what you will do, by when, and what they can expect.

items.label: Follow up
items.detail: Do what you promised and let them know when it is done.

cards.question: A customer says, 'Your service is terrible!' Which reply best acknowledges the feeling without blaming anyone?
options: 'That is not true, sir. Our service is very good.'
'You are right, our technicians are lazy.'
'I can hear how frustrating this has been. Let me look at your file.'
'Please calm down first, then we can talk.'
cards.explanation: Acknowledging the frustration shows you are listening, and moving to the file shows action. Arguing, blaming colleagues or telling someone to calm down usually makes things worse.

cards.title: When your boss is harsh
cards.body:
Some managers speak sharply, especially under pressure. You cannot control their tone, but you can control your response.

- **Separate tone from content.** Ask yourself, 'Behind the harsh words, what is the actual request or problem?'
- **Ask for specifics.** 'Which part of the report needs changing?' turns a vague attack into a task.
- **Answer with facts.** Short, calm, factual replies are hard to argue with.
- **Choose your moment.** If the tone keeps hurting, ask for a short private talk later: 'Sir, can I have five minutes? I want to make sure I understand what you need.'

Staying calm does not mean accepting abuse. Shouting insults, threats or humiliation should be raised with HR or a senior person, following your company's policy.

cards.title: Adds fuel or calms things?
cards.prompt: Sort each response to an angry person by its likely effect.

items.text: 'Calm down, sir.'
Letting them finish before you speak
'That is not my department.'
'I can see why you are upset.'
Rolling your eyes at a colleague
Offering a clear time for the next step
Matching their loud voice
Speaking a little slower and softer

cards.title: Reacting or responding to a rude message
cards.caption: Rude messages tempt us to reply fast. A calm response protects your reputation, because written words stay.

items.label: Speed
items.right: Wait a few minutes; draft first

items.label: Tone
items.left: Sarcasm, capital letters, many exclamation marks
items.right: Polite, short, factual

items.label: Where
items.left: Reply in the big group so everyone sees
items.right: Move to a private message or call

items.label: Goal
items.right: Solve the problem and keep the relationship

cards.title: Midnight blame on the team WhatsApp
cards.situation: It is 11:30 pm. In the office WhatsApp group of forty people, a colleague from the warehouse, Faisal, posts: 'Thanks to customer care, another delivery address is wrong. Great job as usual 👏👏'. Maham entered that order, but she knows the customer changed the address by phone afterwards and the change was passed on.

choices.text: Do not reply in the group tonight. In the morning, message Faisal privately with the facts and suggest a quick call to fix the process.
choices.outcome: Maham sleeps instead of fighting. In the morning, Faisal sees the call log, apologises privately and they agree a simple way to share address changes. The group never becomes a battlefield.

choices.text: Reply in the group straight away: 'Not my mistake. Check your own work before blaming us.'
choices.outcome: Others join in, and the chat turns into a blame war at midnight. Kamran has to step in the next day. Everyone looks unprofessional, including Maham.

choices.text: Post a short neutral line in the group: 'I will check this and update tomorrow,' then follow up privately.
choices.outcome: This calms things and shows she is responsible. It still draws some attention in the group, but she keeps her dignity and solves it the next day.

cards.title: Difficult moment, first calm move
cards.prompt: Match each difficult moment with a good first move.

pairs.left: A customer is shouting at the counter
pairs.right: Let them finish, then acknowledge the feeling
Ask calmly which parts need changing
Wait, draft a short factual reply, and send it only to those who need it

pairs.left: A group chat turns into blame
pairs.right: Move the talk to a private message or call

pairs.left: A colleague is sarcastic in a meeting
pairs.right: Stay neutral now and talk to them privately later

cards.title: Move heated chats to the right place
cards.caption: The bigger the audience, the hotter a disagreement gets. Move it down the funnel to cool it.

items.label: Big group chat
items.detail: Lots of people watching; easy to misread; hard to back down.

items.label: Private message
items.detail: Only the two of you; less pressure to 'win'.

items.label: Phone or voice call
items.detail: Tone of voice helps; misunderstandings clear faster.

items.label: Face to face
items.detail: Best for serious or repeated issues, at a calm time.

items.label: Manager or HR
items.detail: When it cannot be solved between you, or it involves abuse or harassment.

cards.question: Kamran says harshly, 'This report is a mess.' Which reply best separates tone from content?
options: 'You always criticise my work, sir.'
Say nothing and look upset for the rest of the day
'It is not a mess. I worked very hard on it.'
'Which sections should I fix first, and by when?'
cards.explanation: Asking which sections and by when turns a harsh comment into a clear task. It keeps you calm and focused on the work, not on the tone.

cards.title: Usman and the late delivery client
cards.body:
A regular customer of Tariq Printers sends Usman a voice note full of anger: the shop's banner for his store opening arrived one day late.

Usman's first urge is to send an angry voice note back explaining that the customer sent the final design late. Instead he:

1. Listens to the voice note once, then waits ten minutes.
2. Writes a short message: 'I am sorry the banner arrived late for your opening. I understand how important that day was. Can I call you at 4 pm to talk about it?'
3. On the call, he listens first, then calmly explains the timeline and offers a discount on the next order.

The customer stays. Usman never had to win the argument to keep the relationship.

cards.title: Draft, wait, read aloud
cards.body:
Before sending any message written while upset, try this:

- **Draft** it somewhere safe, such as your notes app, not in the chat box.
- **Wait** a few minutes, or until the next morning if it is not urgent.
- **Read it aloud** as if it were going to your most respected senior.

If you would feel embarrassed reading it aloud, soften it or shorten it. Remember: screenshots last for ever.

cards.back: Your safety comes first. Move away, get a supervisor or security, and follow your workplace's safety procedure.
Unwanted comments or messages about your body, gender, religion or personal life are not something to 'stay calm' about. Report them through the proper channel.
Being insulted again and again is not normal feedback. Keep simple notes of dates and words, and speak to HR or a senior person.
Ask a trusted colleague or mentor to help you plan how to raise it.

cards.front: Stress that will not go away
cards.back: If a difficult situation keeps affecting your sleep or mood, speak to a doctor or qualified professional too.

cards.title: Remember from The Storm Counter
items: Most anger at work is about a problem, not about you as a person.
Listen first, acknowledge the feeling, then offer a clear next step.
With a harsh boss, separate the tone from the actual request.
Never fight in a big group chat; move to a private message or call.
Draft, wait and read aloud before sending any message written while upset.
Composure is not tolerance of abuse: threats and harassment must be reported.

cards.prompt: Think of one difficult person you deal with at work, college or in a group chat. What does their behaviour usually trigger in you? Write the first calm sentence you could use next time.

quiz.question: What is usually the best first step with an angry customer?
options: Explain the company rules and policies to them straight away
Let them finish speaking without interrupting
Tell them to calm down
Pass them to a colleague immediately
quiz.explanation: Listening fully shows respect and often lowers the heat. Interrupting, quoting rules or saying 'calm down' tends to make people angrier.

quiz.question: What does 'acknowledging' a customer's feeling mean?
options: Admitting that everything was your fault
Agreeing to every single demand they make so they leave happy
Naming their feeling to show you understand
Repeating their angry words back louder
quiz.explanation: Acknowledging means showing you understand how they feel, for example 'I can see this has been frustrating.' It is not the same as admitting fault.

quiz.question: A message in the office WhatsApp group blames your team unfairly late at night. What is the wisest move?
options: Reply in the group straight away with the facts
Leave the group in protest
Post a screenshot to prove your point
Wait, then follow up privately in the morning
quiz.explanation: Arguing in a big group at night usually spreads the fire. A calm private follow-up the next day solves the problem and protects relationships.

quiz.question: Kamran says, 'This report is rubbish.' Which reply best separates tone from content?
options: 'Which parts should I change first?'
'You never like anything I do, sir.'
'I worked on it all night.'
'Fine, do it yourself then.'
quiz.explanation: Asking which parts to change focuses on the real task behind the harsh words. The other replies react to the tone and usually lead to an argument.

quiz.question: Why is it often helpful to speak a little slower and softer when someone is shouting?
options: It shows that you are not listening
People often match the tone you set without realising it
It makes the other person feel embarrassed about shouting in public
It means you do not need to offer a next step
quiz.explanation: A calm, slower voice often helps the other person lower their voice too. It also helps you stay steady.

quiz.question: Which of these needs reporting through the proper channel rather than just 'staying calm'?
options: A manager asking for a report by Friday
A customer complaining about a late delivery
A colleague disagreeing with your idea politely
Repeated unwanted comments about your personal life
quiz.explanation: Harassment is not a matter of composure. It should be reported to HR or a senior person according to your workplace policy.

quiz.question: In the 'draft, wait, read aloud' rule, why read the message aloud?
options: To check how it would sound to a respected senior
To practise your English pronunciation before sending the message
To make the message longer
To share it with everyone nearby
quiz.explanation: Reading a message aloud, imagining a respected senior hearing it, quickly shows whether the tone is too sharp.

quiz.question: Which response is most likely to add fuel to an angry customer's anger?
options: 'Let me check your file right now.'
'I understand why you are upset.'
'That is not my department.'
'I will call you back by 4 pm with an update.'
quiz.explanation: 'That is not my department' sounds like you do not care. Even if it is true, a better reply is: 'Let me connect you with the right person.'

quiz.question: A disagreement in a big group chat is getting heated. Where should it move first?
options: To an even bigger group, so that more people can join in and help decide
To a private message or a call between the people involved
To social media so others can judge
Nowhere; it is best to keep arguing until someone wins
quiz.explanation: The bigger the audience, the harder it is to back down. Moving to a private message or call cools things down.

quiz.question: Usman's customer sends an angry voice note about a late banner. Which approach best protects the relationship?
options: Send an angry voice note back explaining that the customer was late too
Ignore it until the customer calms down by themselves
Block the customer's number
Wait, send a short caring reply and offer a call to talk it through
quiz.explanation: Waiting, acknowledging the problem and offering a call keeps things calm. Facts can be shared on the call, once the customer feels heard.

sessions.title: Composure Under Pressure: Deadlines, Workload, Priorities and Saying No
sessions.summary: Step up from calming single moments to staying steady through a heavy week. Turn a pile of urgent tasks into a clear plan, agree priorities with your manager, protect focus time and say no politely without damaging relationships. This is how dependable professionals work under pressure.
objectives: Turn a stressful pile of tasks into a written, sorted list
Sort tasks by urgency and importance and decide what to do, schedule, hand over or drop
Ask your manager to confirm priorities when requests clash
Say no or 'not now' politely, with a reason and an alternative
Protect focus time and work on one task at a time

cards.title: Three urgent tasks at once
cards.setting: Zaitoon Electronics, Lahore. The last week of the month, when every report is due.

lines.text: Maham now handles complaints for the whole Lahore region. On Tuesday morning, three things land on her desk within an hour.
Maham, I need the monthly complaints summary by tomorrow. Head office is asking.
Baji, the new refund form is confusing me. Can you sit with me for an hour today?
Then a manager from another branch calls and asks her to join a training session on Wednesday afternoon.
Everything feels urgent. My chest is tight. I keep switching between tasks and finishing none of them.
Pressure is often a planning problem, not a personal weakness. Let us get everything out of your head and onto paper.
Then what?
Then we sort it, check priorities with Kamran and say a polite 'not now' to what does not fit. You will be surprised how much calmer a plan feels.

scenes.heading: Empty your head
scenes.narration: Write every task down: big, small, work, personal. A list on paper feels lighter than a list spinning in your head.

scenes.heading: Sort
scenes.narration: Mark each task: How important is it? How urgent is it? What happens if it waits a day?

scenes.heading: Check with your manager
scenes.narration: When tasks clash, ask: 'Which of these matters most to you today?' Agreeing priorities removes a lot of hidden stress.

scenes.heading: One thing at a time
scenes.narration: Switching between tasks feels busy but often slows you down. Pick one task, close other tabs and work on it for a set time.

scenes.heading: Review and reset
scenes.narration: At the end of the day, tick off what is done and move the rest to tomorrow's list. Leave work with a plan, not a worry.

cards.title: Urgent or important?
cards.caption: Sort each task into a box, then act on the box. Not everything urgent is important.

items.label: Important, not urgent
items.detail: Schedule it: block a time on your calendar, such as preparing next week's training.

items.label: Important and urgent
items.detail: Do it now: the complaints summary head office needs tomorrow.

items.label: Not important, not urgent
items.detail: Drop it or leave it for a quiet day, such as reorganising old folders.

items.label: Urgent, not important
items.detail: Keep it short or hand it over, such as a routine form someone else can complete.

cards.question: Two managers both say their task is 'top priority' for today, and Maham cannot do both. What should she do first?
options: Do whichever task she enjoys more
Stay until midnight and try to finish both
Ask her own manager to confirm which comes first
Do neither until they agree with each other
cards.explanation: When priorities clash, the calm and professional move is to ask the person she reports to which task comes first, and let others know the agreed plan.

cards.title: Saying no without burning bridges
cards.body:
Saying no can feel rude, especially in a culture where we value helping and respecting seniors. But saying yes to everything means doing everything badly. A polite no protects the quality of your work.

- **Thank them:** 'Thank you for thinking of me.'
- **Be honest about your load:** 'I am working on the monthly summary for head office until Wednesday.'
- **Offer an option:** 'I can help on Thursday,' or 'Ali may be able to join instead,' or 'Which task should I move to make space?'
- **Keep it short and warm.** You do not need a long explanation or an apology for having limits.

With your own manager, 'no' often sounds like: 'Yes, I can do that. Which of my other tasks should wait?'

cards.title: Do now, schedule or hand over?
cards.prompt: Sort Maham's tasks into what she should do with each one.

items.text: Monthly complaints summary due tomorrow
Preparing slides for training next week
Re-colouring old spreadsheets to look nicer
A customer refund that must be approved today
Helping Ali learn the refund form
Photocopying forms a junior colleague usually handles
Planning a better complaint process for next quarter

cards.title: The polite no in four parts
cards.caption: Use this pattern for colleagues, other departments and even seniors.

items.label: Thank
items.detail: 'Thank you for asking me.'

items.label: Share your load
items.detail: 'I am finishing the head office report until Wednesday.'

items.label: Offer an option
items.detail: 'I can join on Thursday, or I can send you my notes today.'

items.label: Confirm
items.detail: 'Does that work for you?'

cards.title: The 5 pm request
cards.situation: It is 5 pm on Tuesday. Maham has the head office summary due tomorrow at 10 am and two refunds to approve. Kamran walks over: 'Maham, can you also prepare a list of all repeat complaints since January? I need it for a meeting tomorrow morning.' She feels her chest go tight.

choices.text: Say, 'I can do that, sir. I also have the head office summary due at 10. Which one do you need first, or should the list be shorter?'
choices.outcome: Kamran thinks for a moment and says the summary comes first, and the repeat complaints list can be just the top ten. Maham leaves at a sensible time with a clear plan.

choices.text: Say yes to everything and stay at the office until 11 pm.
choices.outcome: She finishes, but she is exhausted, makes small errors in the summary and is short-tempered the next day. Kamran never learns that her workload was too heavy.

choices.text: Say, 'Sir, I am very busy,' and leave it there.
choices.outcome: This is honest, but it gives Kamran no option and sounds like a refusal. He is annoyed and has to ask again what she can do.

cards.title: Rescuing an overloaded day
cards.prompt: Put these steps for getting control of a heavy day in a sensible order.
steps: Take a slow breath and notice the pressure without panicking
Write every task on one list
Mark each task as urgent, important, both or neither
Check the top priorities with your manager if they clash
Tell anyone affected about changed timelines
Work on the first task with notifications off

cards.title: Panic mode or pressure plan
cards.caption: The same heavy week can feel very different depending on how you handle it.

items.label: Tasks
items.left: Kept in your head, all feel urgent
items.right: Written on one list and sorted

items.label: Focus
items.right: One task at a time, in blocks

items.label: Requests
items.left: Yes to everything, then late on most
items.right: Clear yes, polite 'not now' or a trade-off

items.label: Manager
items.left: Learns about problems at the deadline
items.right: Hears early about clashes and agrees priorities

items.label: Evening
items.right: Tomorrow's list written; mind at rest

cards.question: Which reply is the best example of a polite no to a colleague from another department?
options: 'Sorry, I cannot. I am too busy for this right now.'
'Ask someone else, this is not my job.'
'Okay, fine,' and then not doing it.
'Thanks for asking. I am on a deadline until Wednesday, but I can help on Thursday.'
cards.explanation: A good polite no thanks the person, shares your load briefly and offers a real alternative. Agreeing and then not doing the task damages trust more than an honest no.

cards.title: Maham's polite messages
cards.body:
Here are the messages Maham sent on her heavy Tuesday:

**To the other branch manager:** 'Thank you for inviting me to the training. This week I am finishing the monthly summary for head office, so I cannot join on Wednesday. I would be happy to share my notes on complaint handling, or join a session next week.'

**To Ali:** 'Ali, I really want to help with the refund form. Today is full, but let us sit together tomorrow at 3 pm for 30 minutes. In the meantime, here is the guide I use.'

**To Kamran:** 'Sir, I will send the summary by 10 am tomorrow. The repeat complaints list (top ten) will follow by 12 pm.'

Each message is short, warm and gives a clear time.

cards.title: Protect one focus block a day
cards.body: Pick one block of time each day, even 45 minutes, for your most important task. Put it in your calendar, silence notifications and close your email and WhatsApp on the computer. If someone interrupts, use a holding phrase: 'I am finishing something urgent. Can I come to you at 12?' A single protected block often achieves more than a whole day of switching.

cards.title: Request and polite reply
cards.prompt: Match each request with a calm, polite reply.

pairs.left: Manager adds a new task on a full day
pairs.right: 'Yes, I can. Which task should move to make space?'

pairs.left: Colleague asks for help during your deadline
pairs.right: 'I am on a deadline until 3. Can we look at it at 3:30?'
'Thank you. I cannot join this one, but please share the notes.'

pairs.left: Customer asks for an impossible same-day repair
pairs.right: 'Same day is not possible, but the earliest slot is tomorrow at 10.'

pairs.left: Friend calls about a personal matter during work
pairs.right: 'I am at work now. Can I call you at lunch?'

cards.title: Remember from The Pressure Mill
items: Pressure is often a planning problem, not a personal weakness.
Get every task out of your head and onto one list.
Sort tasks by urgency and importance; not everything urgent matters most.
When priorities clash, ask your manager which comes first.
A polite no thanks, shares your load, offers an option and confirms.
Protect one focus block a day and work on one task at a time.

cards.prompt: Write down everything on your plate this week. Mark each item as do now, schedule, hand over or drop. Which one request do you need to say a polite 'not now' to, and what will you say?

quiz.question: What is the first step in turning pressure into a plan?
options: Write every task down on one list
Start the easiest task straight away
Tell everyone you are too busy
Work late every night this week
quiz.explanation: Getting every task out of your head and onto one list is the first step. It makes the load visible so you can sort it.

quiz.question: In the urgent and important matrix, what should you do with a task that is important but not urgent?
options: Drop it completely
Schedule a time to do it
Do it immediately, before everything else
Hand it to anyone who is free
quiz.explanation: Important but not urgent work, such as planning or training, needs a scheduled time. Otherwise it gets pushed aside until it becomes urgent.

quiz.question: Two people give you clashing 'top priority' tasks. What is the most professional move?
options: Pick the task from the more senior person without telling anyone
Do half of each task
Ask your own manager to confirm the priority and update both people
Ignore both until they sort it out
quiz.explanation: Asking your manager to confirm priorities, then telling both people the plan, is honest and calm. Guessing or ignoring the clash creates more stress later.

quiz.question: Which is the best example of a polite no?
options: 'No. I have too much work.'
'This is not my problem.'
'Sure, no problem at all!' and then quietly never getting round to doing it
'Thanks for asking. I am on a deadline, but I can help on Friday.'
quiz.explanation: A polite no thanks the person, shares your load briefly and offers an alternative. Saying yes and not following through damages trust.

quiz.question: Your manager adds a new task on a day that is already full. What is a good response?
options: 'Yes, I can do that. Which of my other tasks should wait?'
'I cannot do any more work today.'
Agree and quietly drop another task without telling anyone
Complain to colleagues about the new task
quiz.explanation: Saying yes while asking what should wait makes the trade-off clear and lets your manager decide the priority.

quiz.question: Why does constant switching between tasks often make pressure worse?
options: Because managers do not allow it
Because it often slows you down and leaves tasks half finished
Because it uses more electricity
Because it makes every task on your list less important than before
quiz.explanation: Switching feels busy but often wastes time restarting each task. Working on one task at a time usually gets more done with less stress.

quiz.question: Which task belongs in 'hand over or drop'?
options: A customer refund that must be approved today
The head office report due tomorrow
Re-colouring old spreadsheets to make them look nicer
Preparing training slides for next week
quiz.explanation: Re-colouring old spreadsheets is neither urgent nor important. It can be dropped or left for a quiet day.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a daily focus block?
options: To avoid speaking to colleagues all day
To look busy and hard-working in front of the manager
To check social media without interruption
To protect time for your most important task
quiz.explanation: A focus block is a protected time for your most important work, with notifications silenced. It reduces the stress of constant interruptions.

quiz.question: Maham says yes to every request and stays until 11 pm. What is the most likely result?
options: Her manager learns exactly how heavy her workload is
She becomes tired, makes errors and feels more stressed
Her work quality improves because she worked longer
Her colleagues stop asking her for help because she is so busy
quiz.explanation: Saying yes to everything hides the real workload and leads to tiredness and mistakes. Honest, early conversations about priorities work better.

quiz.question: A colleague asks for help during your deadline. Which reply is calm and helpful?
options: 'Can you not see I am busy?'
'Okay,' and then helping for two hours and missing your deadline
Pretend you did not hear the request
'I am on a deadline until 3. Can we look at it at 3:30?'
quiz.explanation: Offering a specific later time keeps the relationship warm and protects your deadline. Snapping or ignoring the request harms trust.

sessions.title: Handling Criticism, Mistakes and Setbacks Without Losing Your Footing
sessions.summary: Go deeper into the moments that shake confidence most: harsh feedback, your own mistakes and setbacks such as a missed promotion. Learn to hear criticism without taking it personally, own errors quickly and professionally, and bounce back with a clear plan. These are the habits senior people notice.
objectives: Listen to criticism fully and separate the useful part from the delivery
Respond to feedback with questions instead of defensiveness
Own a mistake quickly: stop the damage, inform, fix and learn
Write a short, professional message that owns an error without excuses
Recover from a setback using a simple feel, reflect, learn and act cycle

cards.title: The wrong refund
cards.setting: Zaitoon Electronics, Lahore. A Thursday afternoon, during a busy refund week.

lines.text: Maham is checking the day's refunds when she freezes. She approved Rs 18,000 for a customer instead of Rs 8,000.
Oh no. This went out this morning. Kamran will be furious. Maybe nobody will notice...
What would happen if somebody noticed next month instead of today?
It would be much worse. And it would look like I hid it.
Then let us do this the professional way. Stop the damage, tell the right person, give the facts, offer a fix.
Maham calls finance to put a hold on the payment, then walks to Kamran's desk.
Sir, I made an error on a refund this morning: Rs 18,000 instead of Rs 8,000. Finance has put a hold on it. I have changed my checking steps so it does not happen again.
Thank you for telling me straight away, Maham. That is exactly what I need from my team. Send me the details and we will sort it out.

scenes.heading: Stop the damage
scenes.narration: First, limit the harm. Put a hold on a payment, correct a message or call the customer before the problem grows.

scenes.heading: Tell the right person quickly
scenes.narration: Inform your manager or the person affected early. Bad news travels better when it comes from you, and comes soon.

scenes.heading: Facts, not excuses
scenes.narration: Say what happened, when and what the effect was. Keep it short. Explanations can come later if asked.

scenes.heading: Offer a fix
scenes.narration: Say what you have already done and what you suggest next. People remember the fix more than the mistake.

scenes.heading: Learn and adjust
scenes.narration: Change one step in how you work, such as a second check on amounts above a limit, so the same mistake is less likely.

cards.title: Feedback on the work, or a verdict on you?
cards.caption: Criticism usually describes a piece of work or a behaviour. It is rarely a judgement of your whole worth.

items.label: What was said
items.right: 'I am bad at my job.'

items.label: What it is about
items.right: My whole value as a person

items.label: How long it lasts
items.right: Feels permanent

items.label: What to do
items.left: Ask which figures and fix them
items.right: Feel ashamed and avoid the manager

cards.question: Maham finds her own refund error before anyone else does. What is the best first step?
options: Wait and see if anyone notices before saying anything
Put a hold on the payment, then tell her manager straight away
Quietly change the record so the error disappears
Blame the system for showing the wrong number
cards.explanation: Limiting the damage and telling the right person quickly is the professional way to own an error. Hiding or blaming usually turns a small mistake into a trust problem.

cards.title: Hearing criticism without taking it personally
cards.body:
Criticism can sting, even when it is fair. These habits help you stay steady:

- **Listen to the end.** Do not plan your defence while the other person is still speaking.
- **Breathe and thank them.** 'Thank you for telling me' gives you a moment and keeps things calm.
- **Ask for specifics.** 'Can you show me an example?' or 'What would good look like?'
- **Separate the message from the delivery.** Even badly delivered feedback can contain something useful.
- **Take time if needed.** 'Let me think about this and come back with a plan tomorrow.'

You do not have to agree with all of it. You can say calmly, 'I see it a bit differently. Can I explain?' after you have listened.

cards.back: Swap for: 'Thank you. Can you tell me more about that part?'
Swap for: listening to the end, then summarising what you heard.
Swap for: 'This is what I did, and this is what I will do next.'
Swap for: a short follow-up the next day with your plan.
Swap for: 'I got this one part wrong. Here is how I will fix it.'
Swap for: focusing on the content first, then raising the tone privately if it keeps happening.

cards.title: The setback recovery cycle
cards.caption: After a setback, move through these steps. Each time you go round, you come back a little stronger.

items.label: Feel it
items.detail: Allow yourself to feel disappointed for a while. It is normal.

items.label: Reflect
items.detail: Once calmer, ask: what happened, and what was in my control?

items.label: Learn
items.detail: Pick one or two lessons, not a long list of self-blame.

items.label: Adjust
items.detail: Change a habit, ask for feedback or build a missing skill.

items.label: Try again
items.detail: Take the next small step and notice what goes better.

cards.title: Criticised in front of the team
cards.situation: In a team meeting, Kamran puts Maham's weekly report on the screen and says, 'This is careless. The numbers do not match last week's. I expected better from you.' Several colleagues look down at their phones. Maham feels her face burning and her eyes start to sting.

choices.text: Take a slow breath and say, 'Thank you, sir. I will check the numbers today and send a corrected version by 3 pm.' Later, ask for a quick private word about how feedback is shared.
choices.outcome: Maham stays steady and focused on the fix. In the private chat, Kamran agrees he should have raised it one-to-one. The team sees her as someone who can handle pressure.

choices.text: Say, 'Sir, it is not my fault. Finance sent me the wrong data.'
choices.outcome: Even if partly true, it sounds defensive in front of everyone. Kamran pushes back and the meeting becomes tense. The real issue is still not fixed.

choices.text: Stay silent, fix the report later and never mention the meeting again.
choices.outcome: The numbers get fixed, but Maham feels hurt for days and Kamran never learns that public criticism upset her. It may happen again.

cards.title: Owning it, excuses or too harsh on yourself?
cards.prompt: Sort each response to a mistake.

items.text: 'I made an error on the amount. Finance has put a hold on it.'
'The system is so slow, anyone would make mistakes.'
'I am useless. I should not even be in this job.'
'Here is what I have changed so it does not happen again.'
'Nobody trained me properly, so it is not really my fault.'
'I will never be trusted again after this.'
'I am sorry for the trouble. Here is the corrected file.'
'Everyone else makes mistakes too, so why pick on me?'

cards.title: After a big setback
cards.caption: Bouncing back is a process, not a single moment. Give yourself time.

items.label: The first day
items.detail: Feel the disappointment. Talk to someone you trust. Avoid big decisions or angry messages.

items.label: The first week
items.detail: Ask for honest feedback: what could you do differently next time?

items.label: The first month
items.detail: Work on one skill or habit linked to that feedback.

items.label: Next opportunity
items.detail: Go again, better prepared, and notice your progress.

cards.question: Hira was not selected for a team lead post she hoped for. Which response best shows resilience?
options: Decide she will never apply for anything again
Send an angry email to HR about the decision
Tell everyone the selection was unfair
Ask for feedback, pick one skill to build and plan for the next chance
cards.explanation: Resilience means feeling the disappointment, then learning from it and taking a next step. Giving up or reacting angrily closes doors instead of opening them.

cards.title: Maham's mistake email
cards.body:
After telling Kamran in person, Maham follows up in writing so everything is clear:

> **Subject:** Refund error on order 4471: corrected
>
> Sir,
>
> This morning I approved a refund of Rs 18,000 instead of Rs 8,000 for order 4471. I noticed it at 2 pm and finance placed a hold at 2:15 pm, so no extra money has left the account.
>
> The correct refund of Rs 8,000 is now approved. From today I will double-check any refund above Rs 5,000 against the original invoice before approving it.
>
> I am sorry for the trouble.
>
> Maham

Notice what is missing: no long excuses, no blaming the system and no harsh words about herself. Just facts, the fix and the lesson.

cards.title: Talk to yourself like a good friend would
cards.body: After a mistake, notice the voice in your head. Would you say 'You are hopeless' to a friend who made the same error? Probably not. You might say, 'That was a mistake, but you handled it well. What will you do differently?' Use that same kind but honest voice with yourself. Being kind to yourself is not making excuses; it helps you think clearly enough to fix things.

cards.title: Criticism and a calm reply
cards.prompt: Match each piece of criticism with a calm, professional reply.

pairs.right: 'You are right. I will send it by 2 pm and plan earlier next week.'

pairs.left: 'Customers say you sound rushed on calls.'
pairs.right: 'Thank you for telling me. Can you share an example so I can work on it?'
'Which part lost people? I will make that section shorter and clearer.'

pairs.left: 'You made a mistake on this invoice.'
pairs.right: 'Thank you for catching it. I have corrected it and checked the others.'
'I want to meet your expectations. Can we agree what good looks like?'

cards.title: Remember from The Mirror Hall
items: Criticism is usually about one piece of work, not your whole worth.
Listen to the end, thank them and ask for specifics before you respond.
Own mistakes quickly: stop the damage, tell the right person, give facts and a fix.
Avoid both excuses and harsh self-blame; aim for honest and kind.
Bounce back with a cycle: feel it, reflect, learn, adjust and try again.
If public criticism keeps happening, raise it calmly in private.

cards.prompt: Think about a piece of criticism or a mistake that still bothers you. What was the useful part of the message? Write one sentence you could say to yourself, in a kind but honest voice, about it today.

quiz.question: What is the first step when you discover your own mistake?
options: Stop or limit the damage
Wait to see if anyone notices
Write a long apology to everyone
Look for someone else to blame
quiz.explanation: Limiting the damage comes first, for example by putting a payment on hold. Then you tell the right person quickly.

quiz.question: Why is it better to tell your manager about a mistake early?
options: Because managers enjoy hearing bad news
Because it usually means you will not need to fix it
Because it builds trust and stops the problem from growing
Because it makes the mistake disappear from records
quiz.explanation: Early honesty builds trust and gives more options to fix the problem. Hidden mistakes often grow and damage trust when they are found later.

quiz.question: Which reply to criticism is the least defensive?
options: 'Yes, but nobody told me about that.'
'Thank you. Can you show me an example?'
'That is not fair, I worked very hard on this.'
'Everyone else does it the same way.'
quiz.explanation: Thanking the person and asking for an example shows you are open to learning. 'Yes, but' and comparisons with others sound defensive.

quiz.question: Which statement about criticism is most helpful to remember?
options: Criticism always means you are bad at your job
Criticism should always be ignored if it is delivered harshly
Criticism is only useful when it comes from a senior person
Criticism is usually about one piece of work, not your whole worth
quiz.explanation: Seeing criticism as being about a specific piece of work helps you stay calm and focus on the fix.

quiz.question: Which message best owns a mistake professionally?
options: 'Sorry, the system confused me, it is not really my fault.'
'I am so stupid, I always get things wrong.'
'I approved the wrong amount. It is on hold, corrected, and I added a check.'
'Mistakes happen. Let us not make a big deal of it.'
quiz.explanation: A professional message gives the facts, the fix and the lesson. It avoids both excuses and harsh self-blame.

quiz.question: In the setback recovery cycle, what comes after 'Feel it'?
options: Reflect on what happened and what was in your control
Quit and look for a different career
Try again immediately without stopping to think about it
Tell everyone it was not your fault
quiz.explanation: After allowing yourself to feel disappointed, you reflect calmly on what happened before you learn, adjust and try again.

quiz.question: Your manager criticises your report in front of the team. What is the best overall approach?
options: Argue in the meeting to defend your reputation
Leave the meeting to show you are upset
Stay calm, agree to fix the issue, then raise how feedback is shared in private
Say nothing now and complain to colleagues later
quiz.explanation: Staying calm and focusing on the fix protects your reputation. Raising the public delivery privately gives your manager a chance to change it.

quiz.question: Which self-talk after a mistake is both kind and honest?
options: 'I am hopeless and will never improve.'
'It was not my fault at all, the system and the training let me down.'
'It does not matter, nobody cares.'
'I got this wrong, I handled it well, and I know what to change.'
quiz.explanation: Kind but honest self-talk accepts the mistake without harsh judgement and points to a next step.

quiz.question: Which is a 'swap' for the defensive habit of explaining before the other person finishes?
options: Interrupting more politely
Listening to the end, then summarising what you heard
Explaining faster so it takes less time
Writing your full defence in a long email to them instead
quiz.explanation: Listening fully and summarising shows you understood. It lowers tension and makes your later explanation more welcome.

quiz.question: Hira missed out on a promotion. What is the most resilient first week response?
options: Ask for honest feedback about what to work on
Stop doing extra work because it was not noticed
Post about the unfair decision on social media
Apply to every other job she can find that same night
quiz.explanation: Asking for feedback turns a setback into a learning step. Reacting publicly or making hasty decisions often makes things harder.

sessions.title: Lasting Resilience and Leading Calmly: Sleep, Routine, Boundaries, Support and a Steady Team
sessions.summary: Move from getting through hard days to building a steady life at work. Strengthen the foundations of composure (rest, routine, boundaries and people you can lean on) and learn to lead calmly, so that when a crisis hits, your team takes its cue from your steadiness. This is the level expected of supervisors and team leads.
objectives: Build daily foundations for composure: rest, food, movement and routine
Set and explain healthy boundaries on working hours and messages
Grow a support network of mentors, peers, family and professionals
Lead a team calmly through a crisis with clear roles and regular updates
Run a blame-free debrief and recognise when someone needs more support

cards.title: The day the system went down
cards.setting: Zaitoon Electronics, Lahore. Six months later. Maham is now team lead of customer care.

lines.text: At 11 am the billing system crashes across Pakistan. Within minutes, the phone lines are full and customers are queuing at the counter.
Baji, I have five customers waiting and the system will not open! One man is shouting. What do I tell him?
Maham feels the old heat in her face. Then she remembers: her team will copy whatever she does next.
Long breath out. Feet on the floor. First, steady myself. Then, steady them.
Everyone, two minutes, please. The system is down everywhere, not just here. Ali, take names and numbers. Saba, handle the phones with this short message. I will speak to the queue.
Good. I will call head office and update you every thirty minutes.
The room settles. Customers are still unhappy, but the team is calm, and calm spreads.
That is what lasting composure looks like, Maham. Not just your own calm, but a calm your whole team can lean on.

cards.title: Resilience is built on ordinary days

scenes.heading: Rest
scenes.narration: Calm is much harder when you are exhausted. Protecting your sleep where you can is one of the simplest things you can do for your composure.

scenes.heading: Routine
scenes.narration: A steady start and end to the day, such as a set wake-up time and a short evening plan, makes busy weeks feel more manageable.

scenes.heading: Boundaries
scenes.narration: Clear, polite limits on working hours and messages protect your energy and help people know what to expect from you.

scenes.heading: Support
scenes.narration: Mentors, friends, family and colleagues help you see things clearly. Nobody stays steady completely alone.

scenes.heading: Small recovery breaks
scenes.narration: A short walk, a cup of chai away from your screen, or prayer time gives your mind a reset during the day.

cards.title: Foundations of a steady week
cards.caption: Start from the bottom. Each layer supports the one above it.

items.label: Leading calmly
items.detail: Helping others stay steady because you are steady.

items.label: Support network
