items.detail: People you can talk to: mentor, peers, family, professionals.

items.label: Boundaries
items.detail: Clear limits on hours, messages and what you take on.

items.label: Routine
items.detail: Predictable starts, ends and breaks to your working day.

items.label: Rest, food and movement
items.detail: Enough sleep, regular meals and some daily movement.

cards.question: Which of these is the strongest foundation for staying composed week after week?
options: Drinking several cups of tea to keep going late
Answering work messages at any hour to stay ahead
Reasonable rest, regular meals and a steady routine
Keeping all your worries to yourself
cards.explanation: Composure is much easier when the basics are in place: rest, food, movement and routine. Working at all hours and keeping worries to yourself tend to wear you down.

cards.title: Boundaries that protect your calm
cards.body:
A boundary is a clear, polite limit that helps you do good work and stay well. In many workplaces, WhatsApp makes work feel never-ending. Healthy boundaries might include:

- **Working hours:** 'I check messages until 7 pm. Urgent issues can be called in.'
- **Response times:** not every message needs a reply in five minutes.
- **Your workload:** using the polite no from The Pressure Mill.
- **Personal time:** family, prayer, rest and study time matter too.

Explain boundaries kindly and early, and agree them with your manager where needed. Be flexible in real emergencies, but do not let every day become an emergency. Expectations differ between jobs, so follow your contract and company policy.

cards.title: Drains or refills your calm?
cards.prompt: Sort each habit by its usual effect on your composure.

items.text: Checking work WhatsApp in bed at midnight
A short walk or stretch at lunch
Skipping meals on busy days
Talking a problem through with a mentor
Replaying arguments over and over at night
A regular wake-up time most days
Saying yes to every extra task
Writing tomorrow's list before leaving work

cards.title: Leading calmly in a crisis
cards.caption: When things go wrong, the team watches the leader. Use these steps to keep everyone steady.

items.label: Steady yourself first
items.detail: A slow breath and a moment to think before you speak.

items.label: Share what you know
items.detail: Say what has happened, what is not yet known and when the next update will come.

items.label: Give clear roles
items.detail: Tell each person what to do: 'Ali, take names. Saba, handle phones.'

items.label: Update on a rhythm
items.detail: Regular updates, even with no news, stop rumours and panic.

items.label: Debrief without blame
items.detail: Afterwards, ask what worked and what to improve, not who to blame.

cards.title: A team member breaks down
cards.situation: After the system outage, Saba, a quiet member of Maham's team, comes to her desk with tears in her eyes. 'A customer called me useless. I cannot do this job. I keep making mistakes.' Maham has a meeting with Kamran in ten minutes.

choices.text: Move somewhere private, listen for a few minutes, tell Saba the day was hard for everyone, and arrange a proper talk later. If it continues, gently suggest support from HR or a professional.
choices.outcome: Saba feels heard and calmer. In the later talk, Maham learns Saba has been stressed for weeks and helps her reach the company's HR support. Saba later says it made a big difference.

choices.text: Say, 'Do not worry, it is fine,' and go to the meeting.
choices.outcome: It is kind but quick. Saba feels a little better but alone with her worries. A short follow-up later would have helped much more.

choices.text: Tell her, 'You need to be stronger. This is part of the job.'
choices.outcome: Saba feels judged and stops sharing problems with Maham. Her stress grows quietly, and the team learns that it is not safe to speak up.

cards.back: Someone more experienced who can help you think through hard situations, like Nadia does for Maham.
A colleague at your level who understands the daily pressures and can give an honest view.
People who know you outside work and remind you that work is only one part of life.

cards.front: HR or a staff support service
cards.back: Many organisations have HR contacts or support services for staff. Check what yours offers.
For stress, anxiety, low mood or sleep problems that last for weeks or feel too heavy, professional help is the right step.

cards.title: Anxious leader or steady leader?
cards.caption: Teams often mirror the mood of their leader, especially under pressure.

items.label: Voice
items.right: Slower, clear, warm

items.label: Information
items.left: Shares rumours or nothing at all
items.right: Shares what is known and when the next update comes

items.label: Roles
items.left: Everyone does everything, no one knows who does what
items.right: Each person has a clear task

items.label: Mistakes
items.right: Fixes first, learns later

items.label: Afterwards
items.right: Holds a blame-free debrief and thanks the team

cards.question: During a crisis, why should a team lead give updates on a regular rhythm, even when there is no news?
options: To keep everyone busy with messages
Because head office always requires it
So the leader looks important
Because regular updates reduce rumours and uncertainty
cards.explanation: Silence fills up with rumours and worry. A short regular update, even 'no change yet, next update at 12:30', helps a team stay calm and focused.

cards.title: When to get more help
cards.body:
The tools in this course help with everyday workplace stress. They are not a replacement for medical or professional care.

Please speak to a doctor or a qualified mental health professional if you or a colleague:

- feel stressed, anxious or low most days for several weeks
- have ongoing trouble sleeping, eating or concentrating
- feel unable to cope with daily life or work
- have thoughts of harming yourself

If someone is in immediate danger, contact local emergency services straight away. As a leader, you do not need to be a counsellor. Your role is to notice, listen kindly, and help the person reach the right support, while respecting their privacy.

cards.title: Maham's steady-week plan
cards.body:
Maham writes a simple plan on a card and keeps it in her drawer:

- **Mornings:** wake at the same time most days; no work messages until I reach the office.
- **At work:** one focus block before lunch; a ten-minute walk or tea break away from the screen after lunch.
- **Evenings:** write tomorrow's list before leaving; work WhatsApp on silent after 8 pm unless I am on duty.
- **Weekly:** a short catch-up with Nadia every other Friday; one evening with family or friends with my phone away.
- **Team:** a ten-minute huddle every Monday; a blame-free debrief after any big incident.

The plan is not perfect, and some weeks fall apart. But having it means she knows how to get back on track.

cards.title: Running a calm team huddle after an incident
cards.prompt: Put these steps for a blame-free debrief in a sensible order.
steps: Thank the team for how they handled a hard day
Describe briefly what happened, using facts only
Ask what went well and should be kept
Ask what could work better next time, without naming or blaming people
Agree one or two clear changes and who will own them
Check in on how people are feeling and offer support

cards.title: Remember from The Steady Harbour
items: Lasting composure is built on ordinary days: rest, food, movement and routine.
Boundaries are clear, polite limits; explain them early and kindly.
Build a support network: mentor, peers, family, HR and professionals.
In a crisis, steady yourself first, then share facts, give roles and update regularly.
Debrief without blame and check on how people are feeling.
Persistent stress, anxiety or low mood deserves help from a doctor or qualified professional.

cards.prompt: Look at the five layers of the steady week pyramid. Which layer is weakest for you right now? Write one small change you will make this week, and one person you could add to your support network.

quiz.question: Which of these sits at the base of the steady week pyramid?
options: Rest, food and movement
Leading calmly through a crisis
A support network
Saying no politely
quiz.explanation: Everything else rests on the basics: enough sleep, regular meals and some movement. Without them, composure is much harder.

quiz.question: What is a boundary at work?
options: A rule that you never help colleagues
A clear, polite limit that protects your work and wellbeing
A way to avoid difficult or boring tasks that you do not enjoy
A secret list of people you do not like
quiz.explanation: A boundary is a clear, polite limit, such as when you check messages. It is explained openly and helps others know what to expect.

quiz.question: During a system outage, what should a team lead do first?
options: Start calling customers to apologise one by one
Find out whose fault the outage is
Steady themselves before speaking to the team
Leave the team to work it out alone
quiz.explanation: The team will copy the leader's mood. A slow breath and a moment to think comes before giving clear information and roles.

quiz.question: Which habit usually drains your calm the most?
options: A short walk at lunch
Writing tomorrow's list before leaving
A regular wake-up time
Checking work messages in bed at midnight
quiz.explanation: Late-night work messages keep your mind switched on and cut into rest. The other habits tend to refill your calm.

quiz.question: Saba is in tears after a hard day and says she cannot cope. What is the best response from her team lead?
options: Tell her to be stronger because this is part of the job
Listen privately, reassure her, and help her reach further support if it continues
Ignore it so she does not feel embarrassed
Tell the whole team so they can support her
quiz.explanation: Listening privately and kindly, then helping her reach the right support if needed, respects her and her privacy. Judging her or sharing her story harms trust.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a blame-free debrief?
options: To find out exactly which person caused the problem
To learn what worked and what to improve next time
To give the manager a chance to criticise the team
To fill time at the end of the week
quiz.explanation: A blame-free debrief focuses on learning and improvement. When people fear blame, they hide problems instead of sharing them.

quiz.question: A colleague tells you she has felt low and unable to sleep for over a month. What is the most responsible thing to do?
options: Tell her to try harder at breathing exercises
Promise to keep it secret and do nothing
Diagnose the problem yourself
Listen kindly and encourage her to see a doctor or qualified professional
quiz.explanation: Persistent low mood and sleep problems deserve proper help. A colleague's role is to listen and encourage, not to diagnose or ignore.

quiz.question: Why do steady leaders give regular updates during a crisis, even when there is no news?
options: To reduce rumours and uncertainty in the team
Because updates make the crisis end faster for everyone involved
To keep head office busy
So that nobody has to do any work
quiz.explanation: Regular updates fill the silence that rumours and worry would otherwise fill. They help a team stay calm and focused.

quiz.question: Which statement about boundaries is most accurate?
options: Boundaries mean never being flexible, even in emergencies
Boundaries are only for senior managers
Boundaries work best when explained kindly, early and in line with your contract
Boundaries should be kept secret so nobody argues
quiz.explanation: Good boundaries are clear, kind and agreed where needed. They allow for real emergencies without making every day an emergency.

quiz.question: Which member of a support network is the right choice for anxiety that has lasted for weeks?
options: A colleague who tells you to toughen up
A social media group with lots of opinions
Nobody; it is best to keep it to yourself
A doctor or qualified professional
quiz.explanation: Mentors, peers and family are valuable, but persistent anxiety needs help from a doctor or qualified professional.

bank.question: Bilal works at a call centre in Karachi. A trigger log shows he gets irritated most often after 4 pm, when queues are longest, and that his first signal is a tight jaw. What is the most useful next step?
options: Ask to be moved to the night shift straight away
Plan a short reset before 4 pm and watch for jaw tension
Stop keeping the log, because the pattern is now completely clear
Tell customers after 4 pm that he is tired
bank.explanation: A trigger log is useful when it changes what you do. Knowing the time and first signal lets Bilal prepare a reset and catch the reaction early.

bank.question: Which pair correctly places a trigger and a body signal in the stress loop?
options: Trigger: a slow breath out; body signal: an angry email
Trigger: a fast heartbeat; body signal: a deadline moved to today
Trigger: a rude reply-all email; body signal: a hot face
Trigger: typing in capital letters; body signal: a sarcastic comment
bank.explanation: A trigger is the event, such as a rude email. A body signal is the physical response, such as a hot face. Typing in capitals is a reaction.

bank.question: Nida never argues at work and always says 'no problem', but she often cries in the car on the way home and snaps at her family. What is the best description?
options: She is bottling up her feelings rather than handling them
She has excellent composure and should continue
She needs to argue more at work so that the pressure balances out
She is using the STOP pause correctly
bank.explanation: Composure is not silence. When feelings are pushed down at work and leak out later, they are being bottled up, not handled.

bank.question: Why does the stress loop show the 'result' feeding back into the next trigger?
options: Because every reaction makes the next situation calmer
Because results do not matter once the moment has passed
Because the loop only applies to customer calls
Because an angry reaction often creates a new problem that triggers more stress
bank.explanation: A sharp reply, for example, can lead to a complaint or a tense meeting, which then becomes a fresh trigger. Breaking the loop early stops this spiral.

bank.question: A trainer says, 'Composure means you should not feel anything at work.' What is the best correction?
options: Correct: strong feelings are unprofessional
Composure means feeling it and still choosing how to respond
Correct, but only for managers and team leads
Composure means showing every feeling openly so others always know
bank.explanation: Feelings are normal. Composure is about noticing them and choosing a calm, useful response instead of reacting on autopilot.

bank.question: Which situation shows that workplace calm tools are not enough on their own?
options: Feeling nervous before a presentation
Getting irritated when the printer jams just before a meeting starts
Feeling anxious, low and unable to sleep for several weeks
Feeling annoyed by a sharp email
bank.explanation: Everyday stress can be helped by calm tools. Persistent anxiety, low mood or sleep problems deserve support from a doctor or qualified professional.

bank.question: Which is the earliest point at which Maham could break her stress loop during an angry call?
options: After she has shouted, by apologising
After the call, by writing in her log
When she notices her face getting hot
When Kamran tells her the floor heard her
bank.explanation: The earliest chance is when she notices the body signal. Pausing then can stop the reaction before it happens.

bank.question: Imran receives an email at 9 pm that he finds insulting. The issue is not urgent. Which plan is best?
options: Reply at once while the details are fresh
Forward it to the whole team tonight so they can all see how badly he is treated
Draft a reply in his notes app, sleep on it, and reread it before sending
Never reply and avoid the sender in future
bank.explanation: When the matter is not urgent, a draft written safely and reread after a night's sleep usually leads to a calmer, clearer reply.

bank.question: Which statement about the desk breathing pattern in this course is accurate?
options: It must follow exact counts or it will not work
It should be gentle, with a slightly longer out-breath, and stopped if uncomfortable
It cures anxiety for everyone who practises it
It should be done loudly so others know you are calming down
bank.explanation: The course teaches a gentle rhythm, not exact rules, and makes no medical claims. Anyone who feels uncomfortable should stop and breathe normally.

bank.question: Hot thought: 'My manager changed the plan again, so all my work was wasted.' Which reframe is the most balanced?
options: 'He changes things just to annoy me.'
'Nothing I do here ever matters.'
'It is fine, I never really cared about that piece of work anyway, so no problem.'
'Some parts may still be useful. I will ask what the new priority is.'
bank.explanation: A good reframe is fair and useful. It neither pretends everything is fine nor assumes the worst, and it points to a next step.

bank.question: A customer asks a question you cannot answer, and you feel flustered. Which holding phrase is most effective?
options: 'Let me check that and call you back by 3 pm.'
'I do not know, sorry.'
'Why are you asking me this?'
'You should know that already.'
bank.explanation: A holding phrase with a clear time buys you space and builds trust, as long as you follow through.

bank.question: On the 'which calm tool, when?' matrix, which tool best suits a mild feeling when you have plenty of time?
options: An immediate holding phrase on the phone
Writing down the hot thought and finding a fairer version
Leaving the building for the rest of the day
Pressing your feet into the floor while a customer is still on the call
bank.explanation: With time and a mild feeling, you can work through the thought on paper. Quick tools are for moments with little time.

bank.question: What does the 'O' in STOP ask you to do?
options: Offer an apology straight away
Organise your desk and your files before you write any reply
Overrule the other person's point
Observe your feeling, the facts and what you want next
bank.explanation: Observe means noticing your feeling, the facts and your goal before you proceed with a response.

bank.question: Why is reframing different from simply pretending a problem is not there?
options: Reframing keeps the facts but finds a fairer, more useful view of them
Reframing changes the facts themselves so that you can feel better about them
Reframing means blaming someone else for the problem
There is no difference; they are the same thing
bank.explanation: Reframing does not deny the problem. It looks at the same facts in a way that helps you respond calmly and usefully.

bank.question: A customer at the counter shouts, 'You people are cheats!' Which sequence best follows the calming steps from this course?
options: Explain the policy, then listen, then offer a refund
Ask him to lower his voice, listen for a bit, then call security to remove him
Listen, acknowledge his frustration, clarify the facts, then offer a next step
Offer a next step, then explain why he is wrong, then listen
bank.explanation: Listening and acknowledging come first to lower the heat. Clarifying gets the facts right, and a clear next step gives the anger somewhere to go.

bank.question: Kamran says in a rushed tone, 'Fix this, it is embarrassing.' What is the content behind the tone?
options: That Maham is a bad employee who should be replaced
That Kamran dislikes her personally
That she should resign
That something in the work needs correcting
bank.explanation: Separating tone from content shows the real message: something in the work needs fixing. Asking 'which part?' turns it into a clear task.

bank.question: Late at night, a sarcastic message in a 40-person office WhatsApp group blames your team. Which response best protects both the relationship and your reputation?
options: A long, detailed reply in the group straight away that lists every single fact clearly
A screenshot sent to your manager with an angry note
No reply tonight, then a private message or call to the sender the next morning
Leaving the group so you do not have to see it
bank.explanation: Big groups make it hard for anyone to back down. A private, calm follow-up the next day solves the problem with less drama.

bank.question: Which situation should be reported through the proper channel rather than handled only with calm tools?
options: A colleague who disagrees with your idea in a meeting in front of the whole team
A customer who is upset about a delayed repair
A manager who asks for a report to be redone
A colleague who keeps sending unwanted comments about your appearance
bank.explanation: Unwanted personal comments are harassment. Composure does not mean putting up with it; report it to HR or a senior person according to policy.

bank.question: Why does acknowledging a customer's feelings not mean admitting fault?
options: Because it shows you understand their feeling, not who caused the problem
Because customers never notice what you say
Because only managers are ever allowed to admit fault on behalf of the company
Because acknowledging is the same as saying nothing
bank.explanation: 'I can see this is frustrating' shows empathy without accepting blame. It calms the customer while you work out the facts.

bank.question: Usman wants to reply to an angry customer's voice note. Which test helps most before sending?
options: Count how many words the reply has
Read it aloud as if a respected senior will hear it
Send it to five friends first and ask for their opinion on it
Add more exclamation marks to show he cares
bank.explanation: Reading a reply aloud, imagining a respected senior hearing it, quickly shows if the tone is too sharp.

bank.question: A heated disagreement between two colleagues keeps flaring up in the team chat. In the funnel model, when is it right to involve a manager or HR?
options: At the first sign of disagreement
When it cannot be solved between them, or involves abuse or harassment
Only after the argument has already been shared on social media by somebody
Never; adults should always solve it themselves
bank.explanation: Most disagreements cool down when moved to private messages, calls or face-to-face talks. If that fails, or there is abuse or harassment, a manager or HR should help.

bank.question: Maham has three tasks: a head office report due tomorrow, slides for training next week and tidying old folders. Using the urgent and important matrix, what is the best plan?
options: Do the report now, schedule the slides, and leave the folders for a quiet day
Do the folders first because they are quick
Do all three at the same time to save time
Schedule the report and do the slides now
bank.explanation: The report is urgent and important, the slides are important but not urgent, and the folders are neither. Each box has its own action.

bank.question: A senior from another department asks for urgent help on a day already full of deadlines. Which reply best follows the polite no pattern?
options: 'Sorry, I cannot help. I am busy.'
'Okay,' then trying to do everything and missing a deadline
'Ask my manager, it is not my decision.'
'Thank you for asking. I am on two deadlines today; I can help tomorrow at 11. Does that work?'
bank.explanation: The polite no thanks the person, shares the load, offers a real option and confirms. It is honest and keeps the relationship warm.

bank.question: Why is 'Yes, I can do that. Which task should wait?' a useful reply to your own manager?
options: It politely refuses the new task while sounding as though it agrees to do it
It makes the manager do your work
It makes the trade-off visible and lets the manager set the priority
It delays the decision until next week
bank.explanation: Managers often do not know your full load. Asking what should wait makes the trade-off clear and avoids silent overload.

bank.question: Which habit most reduces the stress of constant interruptions?
options: Answering every message within one minute
Keeping email, WhatsApp and calls open all day so nothing is ever missed
Switching tasks whenever something new arrives
Protecting a focus block and using a holding phrase when interrupted
bank.explanation: A protected focus block with notifications off, plus a polite holding phrase, lets you finish important work with less pressure.

bank.question: Ahmed agrees to every request, then quietly misses half the deadlines. What is the main problem with this approach?
options: It shows too much composure
It hides his real workload and damages trust when deadlines are missed
It is the right way to show respect, because seniors should never hear a no
It means he will be promoted faster
bank.explanation: Saying yes and failing to deliver harms trust more than an honest, polite no or a clear trade-off agreed in advance.

bank.question: Two managers each say their task is top priority today. After asking her own manager, Maham is told to do task A first. What should she do next?
options: Do task A and say nothing to the other manager
Do task B first anyway, to keep everyone happy
Tell the other manager the agreed plan and when task B will be done
Ask a colleague to do task B quietly, without telling either of the managers
bank.explanation: Telling the other manager the agreed plan and a realistic time keeps expectations clear and avoids surprises.

bank.question: In 'From pressure to plan', why is writing every task down the first step?
options: Because a visible list can be sorted and feels lighter than tasks spinning in your head
Because managers check your notebook
Because writing tasks down makes them disappear
Because it is quicker than doing the tasks
bank.explanation: A written list turns a vague feeling of pressure into a set of tasks you can sort, prioritise and discuss.

bank.question: Zara notices she sent a customer the wrong delivery date. Put these actions in the best order: (1) tell her supervisor, (2) call the customer with the correct date, (3) add a check to her process.
bank.explanation: First stop the damage by giving the customer the correct date, then tell the supervisor, then change the process so it is less likely to happen again.

bank.question: Which message owns a mistake without excuses or harsh self-blame?
options: 'I sent the wrong date. The customer now has the right one, and I will double-check dates before sending.'
'The system showed the wrong date, so it was not really my fault.'
'I am terrible at this job and always make mistakes.'
'Everyone sends wrong dates sometimes, it is not a big deal.'
bank.explanation: A professional message states the facts, the fix and the lesson. It avoids both blaming others and putting yourself down.

bank.question: A manager says, 'Your presentation was boring.' Which reply best turns vague criticism into something useful?
options: 'Everyone else liked it.'
'Which part lost people? I will tighten that section.'
'I did not have enough time to prepare properly this week.'
'You are always negative about my work.'
bank.explanation: Asking which part lost people turns a vague comment into a specific, fixable point and keeps the tone calm.

bank.question: Kamran criticises Maham's report harshly in front of the team, and it has happened twice before. What is the best follow-up after fixing the report?
options: Complain about Kamran in the team WhatsApp group so that everyone else knows too
Say nothing, because managers can speak however they like
Ask Kamran for a short private talk about how feedback could be shared
Make a mistake in his next report to get even
bank.explanation: Raising the pattern calmly and privately gives Kamran a chance to change how he gives feedback, without embarrassing anyone.

bank.question: In the setback recovery cycle, which step is most often skipped by people who keep repeating the same setback?
options: Feeling the disappointment
Telling friends and family all about it in great detail
Posting about it online
Learning one or two lessons and adjusting a habit
bank.explanation: Without learning and adjusting, people go straight from disappointment to trying again in the same way, and often get the same result.

bank.question: Which inner voice best helps you recover from a mistake?
options: 'You always ruin everything.'
'It was someone else's fault, so there is nothing for you to learn.'
'That was a mistake. You handled it well. What will you change?'
'Forget it, it does not matter.'
bank.explanation: Kind but honest self-talk accepts the mistake, notices what went well and points to a next step. Harshness and denial both block learning.

bank.question: Which defensive habit is being shown when someone starts explaining before the other person has finished giving feedback?
options: Not listening to the end
Separating tone from content
Asking for specifics
Using a holding phrase
bank.explanation: Explaining too early means not listening fully. A better swap is to listen to the end and then summarise what you heard.

bank.question: Which set of habits best supports lasting composure?
options: Skipping lunch to finish early and checking messages late at night
Regular sleep, meals, a short daily break and writing tomorrow's list
Working weekends to stay ahead and avoiding friends to save time
Drinking extra tea to stay awake and replying to every message instantly
bank.explanation: Rest, food, small breaks and a simple routine form the foundation of a steady week. The other habits tend to wear down your calm.

bank.question: Maham explains to her team: 'I check work WhatsApp until 8 pm. If something is urgent after that, please call me.' What is she doing?
options: Refusing to do her job
Being rude to her team
Hiding from her responsibilities as a new team lead after hours
Setting a clear, polite boundary with an emergency option
bank.explanation: A good boundary is clear, polite and allows for real emergencies. It helps people know what to expect.

bank.question: During a branch-wide system outage, which first message from a team lead is most likely to keep the team steady?
options: 'This is a disaster, I do not know what to do!'
'Whose fault is this? Someone must have broken it.'
'The system is down everywhere. Ali takes names, Saba handles phones, next update in 30 minutes.'
Saying nothing until head office sends an update
bank.explanation: Steady leaders share what they know, give clear roles and promise regular updates. Panic, blame or silence spread worry.

bank.question: After an incident, a team lead opens the debrief by asking, 'Who messed this up?' What is the most likely effect?
options: People feel safe to share every problem openly
The team learns faster from the incident
People hide mistakes in future to avoid blame
The incident will never happen again
bank.explanation: Blame makes people hide problems. A blame-free debrief asks what worked and what to improve, so the team can learn.

bank.question: A team member tells you privately that she has felt very low for weeks and finds it hard to get through the day. As her team lead, what is the right approach?
options: Listen kindly, respect her privacy and encourage her to speak to a doctor or qualified professional
Tell her to use breathing exercises and the problem will go away
Share her situation with the team so they can be gentle with her
Tell her that everyone feels like this and she should carry on
bank.explanation: A leader's role is to notice, listen and help someone reach the right support, while respecting privacy. Persistent low mood needs professional help.

bank.question: Which person in a support network is best placed to help you think through a hard situation using more experience than yours?
options: A trusted peer at your level
A mentor
A large social media group
A customer you get on well with
bank.explanation: A mentor has more experience and can help you see options you might miss. Peers and family help in other ways.

bank.question: Why does a leader's composure matter so much during a crisis?
options: Because teams often mirror the leader's mood and behaviour
Because leaders are not allowed to feel stress
Because a calm leader can personally fix any technical problem that comes up
Because customers only speak to leaders
bank.explanation: People take cues from the leader. A steady voice, clear roles and regular updates help a whole team stay calm.
